Lefschetz Fixed-Point Theorem and Lattice Points in Convex Polytopes∗

Sacha Sardo Inﬁrri †

Mathematical Institute 24-29 St. Giles’ Oxford

Abstract

A simple convex lattice polytope ✷ deﬁnes a torus-equivariant line

bundle L✷ over a toric variety X✷.

Atiyah and Bott’s Lefschetz ﬁxed-point theorem is applied to the torus action on the d′′-complex of L✷ and information is obtained about the lattice points of ✷.

In particular an explicit formula is derived, computing the number of lattice points and the volume of ✷ in terms of geometric data at its extreme points. The results of Brion [5] are recovered and an elemen- tary convex geometric interpretation is given by performing Laurent expansions similar to those of Ishida [10].

0

Introduction

0.1 The problem

Let ✷ be a convex polytope all of whose vertices belong to a lattice M. The question of calculating the number of points of M contained in ✷ is a well-known one in convex geometry. The oldest formula appears to be Pick’s classical result [18], valid for arbitrary polygons in 2 dimensions:

1 2 ∗M.S.Classiﬁcation (1991): Primary: 52B20; Secondary: 14M25, 11H06, 11P21. †email:sacha@maths.oxford.ac.uk

#(✷ ∩ M) = Area(✷) +

#(boundary(✷) ∩ M) + 1.

1

Following Ehrhart’s work on Hilbert polynomials, Macdonald [14, 15] sub- sequently generalised Pick’s formula to arbitrary n. His formula expresses the volume of ✷ in terms of the number of lattice points of its’ multiples k✷ for ﬁnitely many integers k. Although these formulae are valid for arbitrary (non-convex) polygons, they do not give any convenient way of calculating either the volume, or the number of lattice points of ✷. A review of this and other problems concerning lattice points can
be found in [8, 7].

From an elementary point of view, for large polytopes one expects the volume to be a good approximation to the number of lattice points, so that one can imagine a general formula of the form

number of points = volume + correction terms

(1)

where the corrections terms are negligible in the large limit. The formula we present here is however quite diﬀerent in nature.

0.2 The results

Given a parameter ζ, to each extreme point α of a simple convex polytope ✷, we associate a rational number depending the local geometry of ✷ at α. Their sum is independent of ζ and yields the number of lattice points in ✷ (Theorem 9). Our main formula (Theorem 6) is more general, since it expresses not just the number, but which points of the lattice belong to the polytope, as a ﬁnite Laurent polynomial in n variables (the lattice points corresponding to the monomials via m 7→ xm = xm1 n ). I

give an initial form of this using the Lefschetz-ﬁxed point theorem for orbifolds. By expanding in Laurent series this is shown to be equivalent to another formulation (Theorem 7) given by Brion [5] which doesn’t involve cyclotomic sums. I use this form to calculate the number of lattice points. The volume of ✷ is obtained by taking the leading order terms for ﬁner and ﬁner subdivisions of the lattice. The Laurent series expansions extend Ishida’s [10] and provide a convex geometric

interpretation of the formula (Theorem 8). This in turn suggests a proof of the formula involving no toric geometry — only convex geometry and elementary Laurent expansions. This could be considered as a variation of Ishida’s proof [10] based on the contractibility of convex sets.

This paper is an ampliﬁcation of my 1990 transfer dissertation at Ox- ford university [20]. This was originally written whilst I was unaware of Michel Brion’s 1988 paper [5], where a toric approach is used to calculate the number of lattice points. There has also been a paper by Ishida [10]

2

where similar Laurent expansions similar to mine are performed. This is the revised version of my original which takes these works into account. Let me brieﬂy mention their relationship to this paper.

Brion relies on the Lefschetz-Rieman-Roch theorem for equivariant K- theory [3] and obtains theorem 7. He calculates the number of lattice points by subdividing the tangent cones into basic cones. The formula that I obtain using the Lefschetz ﬁxed point theorem involves instead cyclotomic sums for the action of the ﬁnite quotient group. By extending Ishida’s Laurent series expansions [10] in section 5 of this article, I prove that the two are equivalent, and provide a combinatorial
interpretation of the formula. It is also not necessary for me to subdivide the tangent cones in order to obtain a formula for the number of lattice points.
0.3 The method

Our main tool is the theory of toric varieties. This associates a holomor- phic line bundle L✷ over a complex orbifold X✷ to any n-dimensional simple polytope ✷ on a lattice M. The variety comes equipped with the action of an algebraic n-torus TN (the character group of M) and L✷ is equivariant with respect to this action. Its cohomology is trivial in positive dimen- sion, whereas its space of sections is naturally isomorphic to a vector space generated by the lattice points in ✷.

In [4, 13], the Rieman-Roch theorem is used to calculate the number of lattice points in ✷. This yields a formula similar to equation (1) above. The problem with this approach, however, is that the correction terms are not readily computable.

In this paper I follow an idea of Atiyah and exploit the torus action. I apply Atiyah & Bott’s Lefschetz ﬁxed point theorem [1] — suitably extended to orbifolds [11] — to the (geometric endomorphism induced by the) action of t ∈ TN on the d′′-complex of L✷. The d′′-complex is elliptic [2] and its cohomology groups are (canonically isomorphic to) those of (X✷,L✷). The ﬁxed points of the torus action on X✷ correspond to the extreme points of ✷. The Lefschetz theorem in this case expresses the

equality between the Lefschetz number (an element of C[M]) and the sum of the indexes να for α in the set of extreme points. The να deﬁne elements of C(M). The formula I obtain initially involves sum over the characters of the ﬁnite abelian groups which charaterise the singularities at the points Pα ∈ X✷ corresponding to α ∈ ext✷. By studying characteristic series for cones in section 5 I eliminate the summation over group elements.

If one restricts t to the one-parameter subgroup of the torus determined by an element ζ of its’ Lie algebra one obtains an equality between a poly- nomial and a sum of rational functions in one variable. When t → 1 the polynomial tends to the the number of lattice points of ✷, and this is given by the sum of the constant terms in the one variable Laurent series for the rational functions: this gives theorem 9. By identifying the coeﬃcient of the leading order terms in the asymptotic expansions
of the formula for sub- multiples of the lattice — the ‘classical limit’ in quantum terminology — I derive a formula for the volume of ✷ in Theorem 10.
I review the toric geometry results I shall need in the ﬁrst part of this paper. The reader who is familiar with the notation in Oda [17] can GOTO PART II, which contains the application proper.

Part I Toric Geometry

The theory of toric varieties establishes correspondances between convex geometry in n real dimensions and the geometry of compactiﬁcations of n-dimensional complex tori. I refer to [12, 17, 6].

Brieﬂy, there is a functor that associates, to a pair (N,Σ) (where Σ is a fan in N), an irreducible normal Hausdorﬀ complex analytic space XN,Σ. A convex polytope ✷ in M determines a unique fan Σ in N, and we set X✷ = XN,Σ. The polytope contains more information than simply its cone structure, and this determines a piecewise linear function h = h✷ on the support |Σ| ⊂ NR of Σ. This corresponds under the functorial construction above to an equivariant line bundle Lh on XN,Σ, which we denote by

1 Cones and Aﬃne Toric Varieties

1.1 Cones

Let V denote a vector space and V ∗ its dual.

A cone in a vector space V is a ﬁnite intersection of half-spaces in V . Cones are always convex and polyhedral. I shall take them to be also strongly convex, namely such that they do not contain any proper subspace of V .

For v1,...,vk ∈ NR, let hv1,...,vki denote the smallest cone containing v1,...,vk. Any cone is generated in this way. A cone is said to be simplicial if it can be generated by linearly independent elements of NR. If it can be generated by part of a Z-basis of N, then the cone is called basic. Finally, a cone is said to be integral with respect to N if it can be generated by elements of N. When we speak of a cone in a lattice N we mean a cone in NR which is integral with respect to N. I only
consider such cones henceforth.
The dimension of a cone is the dimension of the subspace it generates. By the interior of a cone we usually mean the relative interior in the subspace it generates.

1.2 Duality

Given a subset A ⊂ V its dual A∨ ⊂ V ∗ is deﬁned by:

A∨ = {θ ∈ V ∗ : ∀v ∈ V,hθ,vi ≥ 0}.

5

Proposition 1 The dual of a cone (respectively, a simplicial cone, a basic cone, or an integral cone) is a cone (respectively a simplicial cone, a basic cone, or an integral cone). Moreover, for any cone σ we consider, we have σ∨∨ = σ.

For a proof of all the results regarding cones, see [19]. A summary of the results I require will be found in [17].

1.3 Aﬃne Toric Varieties

Let σ be a cone in N. Recall [17, Prop. 1.1] that the subset of M given by

Sσ = M ∩ σ∨

is ﬁnitely generated as an additive semigroup, generates M as a group, and is saturated. Such semigroups are in one-one correspondance with cones in N.

Denote by Uσ = UN,σ the set of semigroup homomorphisms from (Sσ,+)

to (C,·), namely

Uσ = {u : Sσ → C : u(0) = 1,u(m + m′) = u(m)u(m′),∀m,m′ ∈ Sσ}.

This can be given the structure of an n-dimensional irreducible normal com- plex analytic space by choosing generators m1,...,mp for Sσ and embedding Uσ in Cp via the evaluation maps ev(mi) : u 7→ u(mi) on the generators mi. The structure is inherited from the usual structure on Cp and is independent of the generators chosen.

In other words, Uσ is just equal to the (set of points of the) aﬃne scheme Spec(C[Sσ]). Identifying Uσ with its C-points corresponds to identifying ev(m) with e(m). I spend little eﬀort making the distinction. The following proposition is easy to show [17, Th. 1.10]:

Proposition 2 The variety Uσ is non-singular if and only if σ is basic.

2 Fans and General Toric Varieties

2.1 Faces, Fans and Gluing

Let σ be a cone in N.

Deﬁnition 1 A face of σ is a subset of the form σ ∩ {m0}⊥, where m0 ∈ M = hom(N,Z) is non-negative on σ. A face of a cone is also a cone.

6

We immediately have:

Lemma 1 If τ is a face of σ then, for some m0 ∈ M, we have

Uτ = {u ∈ Uσ : u(m0) 6= 0},

so that Uτ is naturally an open subset of Uσ.

Given this, one constructs collections of cones (called fans) which have the property that their corresponding varieties ﬁt together in a natural way:

Deﬁnition 2 A fan in N is a collection Σ = {σ : σ a cone in N} satisfying the following conditions:

if τ is a face of σ and σ ∈ Σ, then τ ∈ Σ.

σ ∩ σ′ is a face of both σ and σ′, for all σ,σ′ ∈ Σ.

The set of cones of Σ of dimension k is called the k-skeleton of Σ and is denoted Σ(k). The union of all the cones of Σ is called the support of Σ and is denoted |Σ| ⊂ NR.

Theorem 1 The toric variety associated to (N,Σ) is the space obtained by gluing together the aﬃne varieties UN,σ for σ ∈ Σ, using lemma 1. It is an n-dimensional Hausdorﬀ complex analytic space XN,Σ which is irreducible and normal [17, Theorem 1.4]. It is compact if and only if Σ is complete, namely if and only if |Σ| = NR.

2.2 The torus action

The torus TN acts on Uσ by (t·u)(m) = t(m)u(m), and this gives an action on XN,Σ. For σ = {0}, one has U{0} = TN, and the action coincides with group multiplication on the torus.

The TN-orbits on XN,Σ are given by the quotient algebraic tori

orb(τ) = homZ(M ∩ τ⊥,C×),

for each τ ∈ Σ. The orbit corresponding to τ has dimension equal to the codimension of τ in NR. It is also easy to see that Uσ decomposes as the disjoint union of the orbits corresponding to its faces, and that orb(σ) is the only closed orbit in Uσ. I record a special case of this for later use:

Lemma 2 The ﬁxed points of the TN action on XN,Σ are in one- one cor- respondance with the orbits orb(σ) ∈ Uσ, for the cones σ in the n-skeleton Σ(n).

2.3 Functoriality

Recall the following characterisation of toric varieties:

X is a toric variety if and only if it is an irreducible normal variety, locally of ﬁnite type over C, with a densely embedded torus whose action on itself extends to the whole variety.

The assignment (N,Σ) 7→ XN,Σ is a functor of categories:

Deﬁnition 3 A map of fans φ : (N′,Σ′) → (N,Σ) is a Z-linear homo- morphism φ : N′ → N whose scalar extension φR : N′ R → NR satisﬁes the following property: for each σ′ ∈ Σ′, there exists σ ∈ Σ such that φR(σ′) ⊂ σ.

Theorem 2 [17, page 19] A map of fans φ : (N′,Σ′) → (N,Σ) gives rise to a holomorphic map

φ∗ : XN′,Σ′ → XN,Σ

whose restriction to the open subset TN′ coincides with the homomorphism of algebraic tori φC× : N′ ⊗Z C× → N ⊗Z C×. Through this homomorphism, φ∗ is (TN′,TN)- equivariant. Conversely any holomorphic map ψ : X′ → X between toric varieties which restricts to a homomorphism χ : T ′ → T on the algebraic tori T ′ and T in such a way that ψ is χ-equivariant corresponds to a unique Z-linear homomorphism f : N′ → N giving rise to a map of fans (N′,Σ′) → (N,Σ) such that f∗ = ψ.

2.4 Finite Quotients

I will be interested in the case when N′ is a Z-submodule of N of ﬁnite index and Σ′ = Σ. I write X′ and X for the corresponding varieties:

Proposition 3 With the data as above, X′ → X coincides with the projec- tion of X′ with respect to natural action of the ﬁnite group

K = N/N′ ∼= homZ(M′/M,C×) = ker[TN′ → TN].

Proof: [17, Cor. 1.16, p.22]

3 Toric Varieties, Equivariant Line Bundles and

Convex Polytopes

3.1 Polytopes

Recall ﬁrst some basic notions of convex geometry.

A convex polytope ✷ in a vector space V is a bounded intersection of a ﬁnite number of aﬃne half- spaces of V . The set of extreme points of ✷ is denoted ext✷. Since ✷ is bounded, it is equal to the convex hull of ext✷. By a polytope on the lattice M we mean a polytope in MR such that ext✷ ⊂ M. Suppose ✷ is such a polytope, and let α be an extreme point. I deﬁne the (tangent) cone of ✷ at α to be the cone Cα in M given by:

Cα = R≥0(✷ − α) = {r(v − α) : r ≥ 0,v ∈ ✷}.

Let λi

α,i = 1,...,k be the shortest generators for Cα which belong to the lattice M. I call these the edges of ✷ emanating from α, or simply the edge vectors for ✷ at α. If Cα is simplicial (respectively, basic), then ✷ is called simple (respectively, basic) at α. Henceforth, all the polytopes we consider are convex, integral and simple at all extreme points. They may be non-basic.

3.2.2 The Variety Deﬁned by a Polytope

I deﬁne X✷ to be XΣ, for Σ = Σ✷. By [17, Theorem 2.22], X✷ is an orbifold (i.e., it has at worst quotient singularities) if ✷ is simple.

Proposition 4 The variety X✷ is compact, and is covered by aﬃne pieces

Uα = Uσα = Spec(C[M ∩ Cα]), for α ∈ ext✷, each containing a unique TN–ﬁxed point Pα = orb(σα) (see equation (2)). Furthermore, when Uα is non-singular, the weights of the TN action on the tangent space TPαUα are given by the edges vectors for ✷ at α.

Proof: The ﬁrst claim follows directly from theorem 1 and lemmas 2 and 3. For the second part, observe (prop. 2 and 1) that Uα is non-singular if and only if the edge vectors at α generate M as a group. The semigroup Cα is then free on these generators. They correspond to the weights of TN on Uα, and hence, by linearity, to the weights on TPαUα.

3.3 Equivariant Line Bundles

The polytope ✷ contains more information than the fan Σ✷. This extra in- formation turns out to be exactly what one needs to specify a TN–equivariant line bundle L✷ over X✷.

3.3.1 Line Bundles and Piecewise Linear Functions

In general (equivalence classes of) equivariant line bundles over XN,Σ are in one-one correspondence with the space PL(N,Σ) of piecewise linear func- tions on (N,Σ), namely functions h : |Σ| → R that are linear on each σ ∈ Σ and which take integer values on the integer points of |Σ|.

Deﬁning an element h ∈ PL(N,Σ) involves, by deﬁnition, specifying an element lσ ∈ M for each σ ∈ Σ such that h(n) = hlσ,ni for all n ∈ σ. These elements determine a line bundle Lh equiped with a TN-action and whose projection Lh → XΣ is equivariant with respect to that action. Note that in general, the elements lσ are not uniquely determined by h, but diﬀerent choices give rise to equivariantly equivalent bundles.

The bundle Lh is deﬁned to be trivial over the varieties Uσ, with transi-

4.2 The Lefschetz Fixed-Point Theorem for Orbifolds

In [11] the Lefschetz formula is generalised to orbifolds (also known as V- manifolds), using zeta-function techniques. As I do not need the full power of this approach, I present an alternative more elementary argument.

The Lefschetz ﬁxed-point formula is essentially local in nature, the for- mula for the multiplicities να only involving the properties of f and φ at the point Pα. 5 Laurent Expansions

In this section I expand the rational functions να away from their poles, i.e., in the domains where |λi α(t)| is not 1, for i = 1,...,n. This has two beneﬁts. Firstly, it produces another formula which does not involve sums over roots of unity. We shall use this in calculating the number of lattice points and the volume.

We don’t attempt this here, as Ishida has al- ready reduced the proof to the contractibility of convex sets [10].
